Thus TD follows given AF (and the unblocked conditions), so AF is sufficient in the logical sense: AF together with the background conditions entails TD.

This is a conjunctive case: the short circuit needs both wires to touch the battery, and removing either one would have prevented it. In that sense the black wire is a genuine cause.

The two wires differ in normality, though. The black wire is supposed to touch the battery, and the red wire is not. Research on causal judgment shows people often single out the norm-violating factor (the red wire) as "the" cause and rate the norm-conforming one lower. That effect is strongest with human agents, as in the pen-taking cases. With inanimate wires it is weaker, and people tend to accept that both necessary conditions contributed.

I expect most people would still say the black wire caused the short circuit, though less readily than they would for the red wire.
